lec05kp23-u01-p1-title.name: u01-p1-title
lec05kp23-u01-p1-title.text: A decision tree draws no boundary but asks yes/no questions, each splitting the data in two

lec05kp23-u01-p1-bridge.name: u01-p1-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p1-bridge.text: The regression of KP22 fitted a line or a curve. Can classification skip the boundary and ask a series of simple yes/no questions?

lec05kp23-u01-p1-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-partition
lec05kp23-u01-p1-fig1.text: Left: two axis-parallel questions cut the plane into regions A, B and C; right: the matching tree, each question testing one feature against a threshold.

image.alt: Left: two axis-parallel questions cut the plane into regions A, B and C; right: the matching tree, each question testing one feature against a threshold.

lec05kp23-u01-p1-term:決策樹.name: term:Decision tree
lec05kp23-u01-p1-term:決策樹.text: **Decision tree**: a series of yes/no questions arranged as a tree. Each circle is a **node** that asks one question; a bottom node that asks no more is a **leaf node** and names the final class. The most common is the OBCT.

lec05kp23-u01-p1-c1.name: u01-p1-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p1-c1.text: **OBCT** (ordinary binary classification tree): each node asks only whether one feature $x_k$ is at most a threshold $\alpha$: \"$x_k\le\alpha$?\"; yes goes one way, no the other.

lec05kp23-u01-p1-c2.name: u01-p1-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p1-c2.text: **Regions** have edges parallel to the axes (rectangles in 2-D). Left: three regions; right: the matching tree.

lec05kp23-u01-p2-title.name: u01-p2-title
lec05kp23-u01-p2-title.text: Four decisions to build a tree; thresholds are midpoints of neighbouring values

lec05kp23-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p2-bridge.text: A decision tree is a series of yes/no questions, each splitting the data in two. To build such a tree, what must be decided first?

lec05kp23-u01-p2-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-cands
lec05kp23-u01-p2-fig1.text: The 10 distinct training values of one feature and the 9 midpoint thresholds between neighbours.

image.alt: The 10 distinct training values of one feature and the 9 midpoint thresholds between neighbours.

lec05kp23-u01-p2-c1.name: u01-p2-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p2-c1.text: **Four decisions**: (1) candidate questions: what each node may ask; (2) splitting criterion: which question is best; (3) stopping rule: when to stop splitting; (4) leaf class: usually the majority.

lec05kp23-u01-p2-c2.name: u01-p2-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p2-c2.text: **Candidate questions**: feature $x_k$ has $N_{tk}$ distinct values in the node; thresholds are midpoints of neighbouring sorted values, so at most $N_{tk}-1$ questions (the textbook says $N_{tk}$).

lec05kp23-u01-p3-title.name: u01-p3-title
lec05kp23-u01-p3-title.text: Impurity measures how mixed a node is: largest when classes are equal, 0 when all are one class

lec05kp23-u01-p3-bridge.name: u01-p3-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p3-bridge.text: The four decisions include a splitting criterion, and there are several candidate questions. By what standard is the best question picked? First we must measure how mixed a node is.

lec05kp23-u01-p3-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-entropy
lec05kp23-u01-p3-fig1.text: The two-class entropy curve peaks at probability 0.5; the impurity is 1.522 for (4,4,2), 1.585 for (1,1,1) and 0 for (5,0,0).

image.alt: The two-class entropy curve peaks at probability 0.5; the impurity is 1.522 for (4,4,2), 1.585 for (1,1,1) and 0 for (5,0,0).

lec05kp23-u01-p3-term:不純度.name: term:Impurity
lec05kp23-u01-p3-term:不純度.text: **Impurity**: a node holding points of several classes is impure; one holding a single class is pure. The impurity $I(t)=-\sum_{i=1}^{M}P(\omega_i|t)\log_2P(\omega_i|t)$ measures this with one number.

lec05kp23-u01-p3-c1.name: u01-p3-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p3-c1.text: **Symbols**: $t$ is the node, $M$ the number of classes; $N_t$ the points in the node, $N_t^i$ those of class $i$, so the proportion is $P(\omega_i|t)=N_t^i/N_t$.

lec05kp23-u01-p3-c2.name: u01-p3-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p3-c2.text: **Properties**: largest when the classes are equal ($\log_2M$); 0 when all are one class ($0\log0=0$). The figure is the two-class curve.

lec05kp23-u01-p4-title.name: u01-p4-title
lec05kp23-u01-p4-title.text: Three nodes worked out: (4,4,2) gives 1.522, (1,1,1) gives 1.585, (5,0,0) gives 0

lec05kp23-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p4-bridge.text: Impurity measures how mixed a node is. Substituting three nodes, what are the numbers?

lec05kp23-u01-p4-c1.name: u01-p4-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p4-c1.text: **Notation**: $(4,4,2)$ means the node holds 4, 4, 2 points of the three classes, $N_t=10$, proportions $P=(0.4,0.4,0.2)$.

lec05kp23-u01-p5-title.name: u01-p5-title
lec05kp23-u01-p5-title.text: Impurity decrease compares questions; the textbook example recomputes to 0.322

lec05kp23-u01-p5-bridge.name: u01-p5-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p5-bridge.text: Three nodes worked out give impurities 1.522, 1.585 and 0. After a question is asked, how are two questions compared?

lec05kp23-u01-p5-term:不純度下降量.name: term:Impurity decrease
lec05kp23-u01-p5-term:不純度下降量.text: **Impurity decrease**: a question splits node $t$ into a \"yes\" child $t_Y$ ($N_{tY}$ points) and a \"no\" child $t_N$ ($N_{tN}$ points); $\Delta I=I(t)-\tfrac{N_{tY}}{N_t}I(t_Y)-\tfrac{N_{tN}}{N_t}I(t_N)$, the largest wins.

lec05kp23-u01-p5-c1.name: u01-p5-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p5-c1.text: **Textbook example**: $t=(4,4,2)$ with $N_t=10$; yes $t_Y=(3,1,0)$ with $N_{tY}=4$; no $t_N=(1,3,2)$ with $N_{tN}=6$.

lec05kp23-u01-p5-c2.name: u01-p5-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p5-c2.text: **Substitute**: $\Delta I=1.522-0.4\times0.811-0.6\times1.459=0.322$. The textbook writes 0.315, not matching its own counts.

lec05kp23-u01-p6-title.name: u01-p6-title
lec05kp23-u01-p6-title.text: Children must be weighted by size: unweighted, a bad split that isolates one point looks good

lec05kp23-u01-p6-bridge.name: u01-p6-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p6-bridge.text: The impurity decrease weights the yes child and the no child by their sizes. Why not simply average them?

lec05kp23-u01-p6-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-split
lec05kp23-u01-p6-fig1.text: A parent of 10 points (5 blue circles, 5 orange squares) split by A into 1 pure point and 9 mixed points, and by B into two groups of 5; box width is proportional to the number of points.

image.alt: A parent of 10 points (5 blue circles, 5 orange squares) split by A into 1 pure point and 9 mixed points, and by B into two groups of 5; box width is proportional to the number of points.

lec05kp23-u01-p6-c1.name: u01-p6-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p6-c1.text: **Two splits compared**: parent $t=(5,5)$ has 10 points, impurity $I(t)=1$. A: yes $(1,0)$ holds 1 point, no $(4,5)$ holds 9; B: yes $(4,1)$ and no $(1,4)$ hold 5 each. The impurity decrease used to compare is $\Delta I=I(t)-\tfrac{N_{tY}}{N_t}I(t_Y)-\tfrac{N_{tN}}{N_t}I(t_N)$.

lec05kp23-u01-p6-c2.name: u01-p6-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p6-c2.text: **Pure point**: a child with only 1 point, all of one class, has $I=0$. A's yes child is a pure point.

lec05kp23-u01-p6-c3.name: u01-p6-c3
lec05kp23-u01-p6-c3.text: **Conclusion**: weighted, B wins (0.278 against 0.108); unweighted, A would win (0.504 against 0.278). A makes only 1 point pure and leaves the other 9, $(4,5)$, almost unimproved.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-title.name: u01-p7-title
lec05kp23-u01-p7-title.text: Impurity left after the split: A leaves 0.892, B leaves 0.722, so weighted picks B

lec05kp23-u01-p7-bridge.name: u01-p7-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p7-bridge.text: A bad split that isolates one point looks good when unweighted. How much impurity does each way of computing leave?

lec05kp23-u01-p7-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-wbars
lec05kp23-u01-p7-fig1.text: Four horizontal bars: the grey bar of length 1 is the parent impurity, the colour is what is left after the split and the gap is the impurity decrease; weighted A 0.108 and B 0.278, unweighted A 0.504 and B 0.278.

image.alt: Four horizontal bars: the grey bar of length 1 is the parent impurity, the colour is what is left after the split and the gap is the impurity decrease; weighted A 0.108 and B 0.278, unweighted A 0.504 and B 0.278.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-c1.name: u01-p7-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p7-c1.text: **First the grey bar**: length 1 is the parent's impurity; the colour is what is left after the split (each piece = share of points $\times$ the child's $I$); the grey gap is $\Delta I$.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-c2.name: u01-p7-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p7-c2.text: **Weighted**: A leaves $0.1\times0+0.9\times0.991=0.892$, $\Delta I=0.108$; B leaves $0.5\times0.722+0.5\times0.722=0.722$, $\Delta I=0.278$.

lec05kp23-u01-p7-c3.name: u01-p7-c3
lec05kp23-u01-p7-c3.text: **Unweighted** (each child counts 1/2): A leaves $(0+0.991)/2=0.496$, $\Delta I=0.504$, fooled by 1 pure point; B is unchanged, 0.278.

lec05kp23-u01-p8-title.name: u01-p8-title
lec05kp23-u01-p8-title.text: Weighted and unweighted worked side by side: A gives 0.108 against 0.504, B gives 0.278 both ways

lec05kp23-u01-p8-bridge.name: u01-p8-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p8-bridge.text: Impurity left after the split is 0.892 for A and 0.722 for B. How does the arithmetic work out weighted and unweighted?

lec05kp23-u01-p8-c1.name: u01-p8-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p8-c1.text: **How to read**: $\Delta I=I(t)-\tfrac{N_{tY}}{N_t}I(t_Y)-\tfrac{N_{tN}}{N_t}I(t_N)$ with parent $I(t)=1$. Each row is one split; a child is written \"points: impurity\".

lec05kp23-u01-p9-title.name: u01-p9-title
lec05kp23-u01-p9-title.text: As the tree grows, training accuracy reaches 100% but new data stalls near 85%

lec05kp23-u01-p9-bridge.name: u01-p9-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p9-bridge.text: Weighted and unweighted worked side by side picked B and A. Weighted splits can go on and on; what happens when the tree is too big?

lec05kp23-u01-p9-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-depth
lec05kp23-u01-p9-fig1.text: Training and new-point accuracy of trees of depth 1 to 12 on two-moon data: training reaches 100% while new points stay near 85%.

image.alt: Training and new-point accuracy of trees of depth 1 to 12 on two-moon data: training reaches 100% while new points stay near 85%.

lec05kp23-u01-p9-term:過擬合.name: term:Overfitting
lec05kp23-u01-p9-term:過擬合.text: **Depth** is how many questions are asked from the top; **leaves** is the number of final leaf nodes. **Overfitting**: the model learns even the details of the training data; the training score is high but new data stops improving.

lec05kp23-u01-p9-c1.name: u01-p9-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p9-c1.text: **Data**: two noisy half-moons (standard deviation 0.35), 200 training points (100 per class) and 2000 new points (1000 per class); entropy criterion.

lec05kp23-u01-p9-c2.name: u01-p9-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p9-c2.text: **Watch the gap**: training minus new points. Depth 1: $76.5-73.3=3.2$ points; depth 12: $100-85.1=14.9$. The gap widens and new points stop improving.

lec05kp23-u01-p10-title.name: u01-p10-title
lec05kp23-u01-p10-title.text: Right counts and accuracy at each depth: training reaches 100%, new points stall near 85%

lec05kp23-u01-p10-bridge.name: u01-p10-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p10-bridge.text: As the tree grows, training accuracy reaches 100% but new data stalls near 85%. Where does each number come from?

lec05kp23-u01-p10-c1.name: u01-p10-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p10-c1.text: **How to read**: \"153 → 76.5%\" means 153 of 200 training points are right, $153/200=76.5\%$; of 2000 new points $1466/2000=73.3\%$. Depth: questions asked from the top; leaves: final leaf nodes.

lec05kp23-u01-p11-title.name: u01-p11-title
lec05kp23-u01-p11-title.text: Grow first, then prune: from 24 leaves to 10, accuracy on new data rises from 85.1% to 87.3%

lec05kp23-u01-p11-bridge.name: u01-p11-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p11-bridge.text: The right counts at each depth show training reaching 100% while new points stall near 85%. How is a tree that grew too large trimmed?

lec05kp23-u01-p11-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-prune
lec05kp23-u01-p11-fig1.text: Pruning strengths 0, 0.01, 0.02 and 0.05 leave 24, 22, 10 and 7 leaves with 85.1%, 85.1%, 87.3% and 86.3% on new points.

image.alt: Pruning strengths 0, 0.01, 0.02 and 0.05 leave 24, 22, 10 and 7 leaves with 85.1%, 85.1%, 87.3% and 86.3% on new points.

lec05kp23-u01-p11-term:剪枝.name: term:Pruning
lec05kp23-u01-p11-term:剪枝.text: **Pruning**: grow a big tree first, then cut off branches that are not worth it. Cost-complexity pruning minimizes \"total impurity $+\ \alpha\times$ leaves\"; the larger the pruning strength $\alpha$, the harder it cuts.

lec05kp23-u01-p11-c1.name: u01-p11-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p11-c1.text: **The same data** (200 training points, 2000 new points, entropy criterion); only $\alpha$ changes.

lec05kp23-u01-p11-c2.name: u01-p11-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p11-c2.text: **Read**: with 10 leaves new points get $1746/2000=87.3\%$, better than unpruned $1702/2000=85.1\%$; pruning too hard (7 leaves) falls a little. One data set, one experiment.

lec05kp23-u01-p12-title.name: u01-p12-title
lec05kp23-u01-p12-title.text: The harder the pruning the fewer the leaves: 24 down to 7, best new points 87.3%

lec05kp23-u01-p12-bridge.name: u01-p12-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p12-bridge.text: The right counts for each alpha show the best new-point accuracy at 10 leaves. What are they?

lec05kp23-u01-p12-c1.name: u01-p12-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p12-c1.text: **How to read**: the same 200 training and 2000 new points; $\alpha$ is the pruning strength. \"193 → 96.5%\" is training $193/200=96.5\%$; \"1746 → 87.3%\" is new points $1746/2000=87.3\%$.

lec05kp23-u01-p13-title.name: u01-p13-title
lec05kp23-u01-p13-title.text: A new training set grows a different tree: the first threshold jumps between 0.09 and 0.42

lec05kp23-u01-p13-bridge.name: u01-p13-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p13-bridge.text: The harder the pruning the fewer the leaves, with best new points at 10 leaves. Does the tree grow the same on a different training set?

lec05kp23-u01-p13-term:高變異.name: term:High variance
lec05kp23-u01-p13-term:高變異.text: **High variance**: slightly different training data grow very different trees.

lec05kp23-u01-p13-c1.name: u01-p13-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p13-c1.text: **Experiment**: grow an unlimited-depth tree on each of 8 training sets of 200 points. The first cut (the question at the very top) always uses the second feature but the thresholds are 0.42, 0.11, 0.12, 0.09, 0.22, 0.26, 0.22, 0.29; the leaves number 22 to 33.

lec05kp23-u01-p13-c2.name: u01-p13-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p13-c2.text: **Why**: a tree is hierarchical, so one error high up spreads to every leaf below.

lec05kp23-u01-p14-title.name: u01-p14-title
lec05kp23-u01-p14-title.text: Averaging the votes of 25 trees lifts new data from 84.4% to 87.7%

lec05kp23-u01-p14-bridge.name: u01-p14-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p14-bridge.text: High variance makes the first threshold jump around. Can the votes of many trees lower the variance?

lec05kp23-u01-p14-term:Bagging.name: term:Bagging
lec05kp23-u01-p14-term:Bagging.text: **Bagging**: draw $B$ sets from the training set **with replacement** (as large as the original, some points repeated, some missed), grow a tree on each and take a majority vote. A **random forest** adds a trick: each node chooses only among randomly picked features (here just 1 at a time).

lec05kp23-u01-p14-c1.name: u01-p14-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p14-c1.text: **Experiment**: 20 different training sets (seeds 100 to 119), $B=25$ trees; 2000 new points. The errors of many trees differ and cancel in the vote.

lec05kp23-u01-p15-title.name: u01-p15-title
lec05kp23-u01-p15-title.text: Extension: one slanted line suffices; axis-parallel trees need 13 to 14 leaves

lec05kp23-u01-p15-bridge.name: u01-p15-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p15-bridge.text: Averaging the votes of 25 trees lowered the variance. Extension: when the boundary is a slanted line, what happens to axis-parallel trees?

lec05kp23-u01-p15-fig1.name: fig:lec05-kp23-oblique
lec05kp23-u01-p15-fig1.text: The class is set by the line x₁+x₂=0: axis-parallel trees of depth 1, 3 and 6 have 2, 7 and 13 leaves with 75.0%, 89.6% and 95.4% on new points.

image.alt: The class is set by the line x₁+x₂=0: axis-parallel trees of depth 1, 3 and 6 have 2, 7 and 13 leaves with 75.0%, 89.6% and 95.4% on new points.

lec05kp23-u01-p15-c1.name: u01-p15-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p15-c1.text: **Data**: 300 training points uniform on $[-1,1]^2$, the class decided by $x_1+x_2>0$; 3000 new points. One oblique question \"$x_1+x_2\le0$?\" separates them exactly.

lec05kp23-u01-p15-c2.name: u01-p15-c2
lec05kp23-u01-p15-c2.text: **An axis-parallel tree** needs many cuts (a staircase) to approximate the line; oblique questions cut well but are harder to train (source).

lec05kp23-u01-p16-title.name: u01-p16-title
lec05kp23-u01-p16-title.text: Extension: axis-parallel trees need 13 to 14 leaves to near the line

lec05kp23-u01-p16-bridge.name: u01-p16-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p16-bridge.text: The axis-parallel tree approximates the slanted line with a staircase. What are the right counts at each depth?

lec05kp23-u01-p16-c1.name: u01-p16-c1
lec05kp23-u01-p16-c1.text: **How to read**: 300 training points and 3000 new points; \"2687 → 89.6%\" is $2687/3000=89.6\%$. Training accuracy is written directly as a percentage.

lec05kp23-u01-p17-title.name: u01-p17-title
lec05kp23-u01-p17-title.text: Extension: exercise, comparing the impurity decrease of two splits

lec05kp23-u01-p17-bridge.name: u01-p17-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p17-bridge.text: Extension: axis-parallel trees need many cuts on a slanted line. One exercise checks how the impurity decrease is computed; can you work it out yourself?

lec05kp23-u01-p17-q1.name: u01-p17-q1
lec05kp23-u01-p17-q1.text: **Exercise**: node $t=(4,4)$ (4 points of class one and 4 of class two), $N_t=8$, $I(t)=1$. Split A: yes $(3,1)$, no $(1,3)$; split B: yes $(2,2)$, no $(2,2)$. Given $I(3,1)=0.811$.

lec05kp23-u01-p17-q2.name: u01-p17-q2
lec05kp23-u01-p17-q2.text: **Ask**: (1) what is $\Delta I=I(t)-\tfrac{N_{tY}}{N_t}I(t_Y)-\tfrac{N_{tN}}{N_t}I(t_N)$ for split A? (2) for split B? Which split is better?

lec05kp23-u01-p18-title.name: u01-p18-title
lec05kp23-u01-p18-title.text: Extension: split A has impurity decrease 0.189, split B has 0, so A is better

lec05kp23-u01-p18-bridge.name: u01-p18-bridge
lec05kp23-u01-p18-bridge.text: Extension: the exercise asked the impurity decrease of two splits. Worked out in full, which is better?

lec05kp23-u01-p18-a1.name: u01-p18-a1
lec05kp23-u01-p18-a1.text: **(1)** Split A: both children hold 4 points with $I=0.811$, so $\Delta I=1-\tfrac48\cdot0.811-\tfrac48\cdot0.811=0.189$.

lec05kp23-u01-p18-a2.name: u01-p18-a2
lec05kp23-u01-p18-a2.text: **(2)** Split B: both children are $(2,2)$ with $I=1$, so $\Delta I=1-\tfrac48\cdot1-\tfrac48\cdot1=0$.

lec05kp23-u01-p18-a3.name: u01-p18-a3
lec05kp23-u01-p18-a3.text: **Check**: A is better; B lowers the impurity not at all. A split into $(4,0)$ and $(0,4)$ would give $\Delta I=1$, the maximum.

steps.label: Decision trees
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the new lecture lec05-kp23; every page is self-contained: the symbols, terms and formulas it uses are restated on the same page, so no flipping back is needed. Main line 9 pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed). Self-study deck, English version. All experiments were recomputed by a program; the data generators, seeds and sizes are in the page notes and the lecture; the numbers of the textbook's Example 4.2 differ from a recount of its own counts, which the page points out. Speaker notes contain no student numbers, grades or exam items.

steps.label: A series of yes/no questions
steps.speakerNotes: The regression of KP22 fitted a line or a curve. This page asks whether classification can skip the boundary and ask a series of simple yes/no questions. A decision tree arranges such questions as a tree: each circle is a node that asks one question, and a bottom node that asks no more is a leaf node naming the final class. The most common one is the ordinary binary classification tree: each node asks whether one feature is at most a threshold, yes goes one way and no the other, so the regions have edges parallel to the axes. The left of the figure shows three regions and the right the matching tree, each inner node matching one cut on the left. The next page asks what must be decided to build a tree.

steps.label: Four decisions
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, A series of yes/no questions. A tree is made of a series of yes/no questions. This page asks what must be decided to build one. Four things: what each node may ask, which question is best, when to stop, and how a leaf decides its class, usually by majority. Where do candidate questions come from? A feature has some distinct values in the node; sort them and take the midpoint of each neighbouring pair as a threshold, so there are at most one fewer than the number of distinct values; the textbook writes the same number. Example: ten values give exactly nine midpoints, for instance 1.2 between 1.0 and 1.4; the figure shows the ten values and the nine midpoints. The next page asks by what standard the best of these many questions is chosen; first we need to measure how mixed a node is.

steps.label: Impurity
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Four decisions. There are several candidate questions and more than one feature. This page asks by what standard the best question is picked; first we must measure how mixed a node is. A node holding points of several classes is impure, one holding a single class is pure. The impurity is the Shannon entropy: take each class's proportion in the node, multiply by its base-2 logarithm, add them up and negate; the proportion is the number of points of that class divided by the number of points in the node. Properties: largest when the classes are equal, the base-2 log of M for M classes; 0 when all are one class. The figure is the two-class entropy curve, highest, 1, when the two classes are half and half. The next page works the formula through on three nodes, step by step.

steps.label: Impurity examples
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Impurity. The impurity formula uses proportions and base-2 logarithms. This page substitutes three nodes. Notation first: (4,4,2) means the node holds 4, 4 and 2 points of the three classes, 10 in all, with proportions 0.4, 0.4 and 0.2. Step one: minus 0.4 times the base-2 log of 0.4 is 0.529, and there are two of them; step two: the same for 0.2 is 0.464; step three: add, 2 times 0.529 plus 0.464 is 1.522, which the textbook writes as 1.521, a rounding difference. One point in each of three classes gives the base-2 log of 3, 1.585, the maximum for three classes; all one class gives 0. The next page asks how to compare two questions to see which splits better.

steps.label: Impurity decrease
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Impurity examples. Impurity was computed for three nodes. This page asks how, after a question is asked, two questions are compared. Look at how much impurity falls after the split: node t splits into a yes child and a no child, multiply each child's impurity by its share of the points, add them, and subtract from the impurity t had; that is the impurity decrease, and the question with the largest one wins. The textbook example: t is (4,4,2), 10 points; the yes child (3,1,0) has 4 and the no child (1,3,2) has 6. Substituting: 1.522 minus 0.4 times 0.811 minus 0.6 times 1.459 equals 0.322. The textbook writes 0.315, which does not match its own counts; only this one split was recomputed here. The next page asks why the children are multiplied by their size shares and not simply averaged.

steps.label: Why weight
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Impurity decrease. The impurity decrease multiplies each child's impurity by its share of the points. This page asks why it cannot simply be averaged. A small example: the parent has five points of class one and five of class two, impurity 1. Split A cuts one point off on its own and the other nine, (4,5), are still mixed; split B halves the ten points into (4,1) and (1,4). Weighted: A is 1 minus 0.1 times 0 minus 0.9 times 0.991, which is 0.108; B is 1 minus 0.5 times 0.722 minus 0.5 times 0.722, which is 0.278, so B wins. Unweighted, a plain average: A is 1 minus (0 plus 0.991) over 2, which is 0.504, B stays 0.278, so A would win and one pure point is mistaken for a big gain. The next page asks how large the tree should grow when splitting goes on.

steps.label: Impurity left
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Why weight. The Why weight figure showed A isolating one pure point. This page draws the impurity left as bars: the grey bar of length 1 is the parent's impurity, the colour is what is left after the split, each piece being the share of points times the child's impurity, and the grey gap is the impurity decrease. Weighted, A leaves 0.892 and the gap is only 0.108; B leaves 0.722 with a gap of 0.278, so B wins. Unweighted, each child counts one half, A leaves 0.496, the gap is 0.504 and one pure point fools the rule. The next page lists the weighted and unweighted arithmetic as a table.

steps.label: Weighting worked
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Impurity left. In the Why weight example A isolates one point and B halves the data. This page works both ways of computing. Each table row is one split: the yes and no children, each with its points and impurity. A: 1 minus 0.1 times 0 minus 0.9 times 0.991 is 0.108; unweighted it is 1 minus (0 plus 0.991) over 2, 0.504. B: 1 minus 0.5 times 0.722 minus 0.5 times 0.722 is 0.278, the same weighted or not. So weighted picks B and unweighted picks A. The next page asks how large the tree should grow as splitting goes on.

steps.label: How big a tree
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Weighting worked. Weighted splits can go on and on, growing even leaves of one point. This page asks what happens when the tree is too big. Two terms first: depth is how many questions are asked from the top and leaves is the number of final leaf nodes; overfitting is the model learning even the details of the training data, so the training score is high while new data stops improving. Data: two noisy half-moons, 100 training points per class and 1000 new points per class, scikit-learn, a single draw with seeds 1 and 2. Each table row is correct over total: depth 1 has training 153 over 200, 76.5%, and new points 1466 over 2000, 73.3%. As the leaves grow, training climbs to 100% and new points stall near 85%, the gap growing from 3.2 to 14.9 points. The next page asks how to trim a tree that grew too large.

steps.label: How big: numbers
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, How big a tree. The How big a tree figure showed training reaching 100% and new data stalling near 85%. Where does each number come from? Each row is a tree whose maximum depth is limited: how many of the 200 training points and how many of the 2000 new points it gets right, divided by the totals. Depth 1: training 153 over 200 is 76.5%, new points 1466 over 2000 is 73.3%, a gap of 3.2 points; depth 12: training 100%, new points 85.1%, a gap of 14.9. A gap that keeps widening is a sign of overfitting. The next page asks how to trim a tree that grew too large.

steps.label: Pruning
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, How big: numbers. A tree of 24 leaves reaches only about 85% on new data. This page asks how a tree that grew too large is trimmed. Pruning first: grow a big tree, then cut off branches that are not worth it. Here we use cost-complexity pruning, which minimizes total impurity plus alpha times the number of leaves; alpha is the pruning strength, the larger the harder the cut. The textbook says that a rule such as stopping when the impurity decrease is small often stops too early or too late, hence grow first and prune afterwards. On the same training and new data, changing only alpha: alpha 0 keeps 24 leaves, new points 1702 over 2000, 85.1%; alpha 0.02 leaves 10, new points 1746 over 2000, 87.3%; 0.05 leaves 7, 86.3%. Also, entropy and Gini over 20 different training sets each give 86.1% on new points, so the choice of criterion hardly matters. The next page asks whether the tree grows the same on a different training set.

steps.label: Pruning: numbers
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Pruning. The Pruning figure showed the highest new-data accuracy at 10 leaves. This page lists the right counts for each alpha. Alpha 0 means no pruning: 24 leaves, training all right, new points 1702 over 2000, 85.1%; alpha 0.02 leaves 10 leaves, training 193 over 200, 96.5%, new points 1746 over 2000, 87.3%; 0.05 leaves 7, new points 86.3%. The training score falls while new data improves, which is the benefit of pruning, but cutting too hard lowers it again. The next page asks whether the tree grows the same on a different training set.

steps.label: High variance
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Pruning: numbers. Pruning trimmed one tree. This page asks whether, on a different training set, the tree grows the same. Grow an unlimited-depth tree on each of eight training sets of 200 points, seeds 40 to 47: the first cut always uses the second feature, but the thresholds are 0.42, 0.11, 0.12, 0.09, 0.22, 0.26, 0.22, 0.29, with 22 to 33 leaves. A small difference in the data grows a different tree, which is called high variance, because a tree is hierarchical and one error high up spreads to every leaf below. The next page asks whether the votes of many trees can lower the variance.

steps.label: Bagging
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, High variance. High variance makes the first threshold jump around. This page asks whether the votes of many trees can lower the variance. Bagging: draw B sets from the training set with replacement, each as large as the original with some points repeated and some missed, grow a tree on each and take a majority vote; a random forest adds that each node chooses only among randomly picked features. The experiment uses twenty different training sets and B equal to 25: a single tree 84.4% plus or minus 1.4, bagging 87.7% plus or minus 1.1, random forest 87.8% plus or minus 1.1. The errors of many trees differ and cancel in the vote, lowering the variance. The next page is an extension: what happens when axis-parallel trees meet a slanted line.

steps.label: Extension: oblique
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Bagging. Bagging made the trees steadier. This page is an extension: when the boundary is a slanted line, what happens to axis-parallel trees? Three hundred training points are uniform in the square from minus 1 to 1, the class decided by whether x1 plus x2 is above 0, with 3000 new points. One oblique question, x1 plus x2 at most 0, separates them exactly; but an axis-parallel tree can only cut parallel to the axes and needs a staircase of many cuts: depth 1 has 2 leaves and 75.0% on new points; depth 6 has 13 leaves and 2863 over 3000, 95.4%; the full tree has 14 leaves and 95.1%. Oblique questions cut well but are harder to train, as the source says. The next page is the exercise.

steps.label: Extension: oblique numbers
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Extension: oblique. Extension: the oblique figure showed the axis-parallel tree approximating the slanted line with a staircase. This page lists the right counts at each depth: depth 1 has two leaves and new points 2251 over 3000, 75.0%; depth 3 has seven leaves, 89.6%; depth 6 has thirteen leaves, 2863 over 3000, 95.4%; the unlimited tree has 14 leaves, 95.1%. It takes 13 to 14 leaves to reach about 95%, while one slanted line is enough. The next page is the exercise.

steps.label: Extension: exercise
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Extension: oblique numbers. In the extension axis-parallel trees needed many cuts on a slanted line. One exercise checks how the impurity decrease is computed; can you work it out yourself? The node is (4,4), 8 points, impurity 1. Split A has yes and no children (3,1) and (1,3); split B has two (2,2). Given that the impurity of (3,1) is 0.811. What is the impurity decrease of A and of B, and which is better? Try it yourself before the worked solution on the next page.

steps.label: Extension: solution
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Extension: exercise. The exercise asked the impurity decrease of two splits; worked out in full. Split A has two children of 4 points each with impurity 0.811, so 1 minus 4 over 8 times 0.811 minus 4 over 8 times 0.811 equals 0.189. Split B has two children (2,2) with impurity 1, so 1 minus 0.5 minus 0.5 equals 0. Check: A is better and B lowers the impurity not at all; a split into (4,0) and (0,4) would give a decrease of 1, the maximum. That ends decision trees; the next KP covers combining classifiers.
